status: Draft from the mishnah, R. Kulp and Kehati.

principles.t: An animal is an attested danger (mu'ad) for what is its way (breaking as it walks, eating what it likes). In an unusual way it is harmless (tam) and the owner pays half.
For tooth (shen) and foot (regel), the owner is exempt in the public domain (except for what the animal benefited) and pays in the domain of the damaged party.
An animal becomes an attested danger (mu'ad) by repeated damage with testimony, and returns to harmless (tam) when it is safe with children.
A conclusion drawn by reasoning cannot be stricter than the law it is drawn from (dayo): half damages for horn (keren) in the injured party's domain.
A person is always an attested danger (mu'ad): full damages for damage (nezek), accident or not, awake or asleep.

terms.def: Damage by an animal's trampling as it walks. An attested danger in its usual way.
Damage by an animal's eating. An attested danger to eat what is fit for it.
Damage by goring and similar unusual damage. Harmless unless the animal has become an attested danger.
The rule that a conclusion from reasoning is not stricter than its source.

debates.title: How does an ox become an attested danger?
debates.a: Rabbi Judah: testimony on three days; harmless again after three days without damage.
debates.b: Rabbi Meir: testimony three times; harmless again when children can touch it. Halakha: R. Judah for becoming, R. Meir for returning.

debates.title: How much does a harmless ox pay in the injured party's domain?
debates.a: Rabbi Tarfon: full damages, by an argument from tooth and foot.
debates.b: The Sages: half damages, since the conclusion may not exceed its source (dayo). Halakha: the Sages.
